name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q01 - Variation of atomic radius across period

questiontext.text:
The graph below illustrates the variation of atomic radius with atomic number (\(Z\)) for the second-period elements from lithium (\(Z=3\)) to fluorine (\(Z=9\)):

Which statement best accounts for the continuous decrease in atomic radius observed from lithium to fluorine across the second period?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the trend depicted in the diagram
The plot indicates that as atomic number \(Z\) increases from 3 to 9 in the second period, the atomic radius decreases continuously from 152 pm in lithium to 64 pm in fluorine.

Step 2: Analysis of nuclear charge and electronic shielding
Across a period, successive electrons are added into orbitals of the same principal energy shell (\(n = 2\)). Because incoming electrons enter the same valence level, the shielding of the nuclear charge provided by inner core electrons does not increase significantly.

Step 3: Determination of the net electrostatic effect
With each added proton, the nuclear charge increases by \(+1\). This steady increase in nuclear charge outweighs the minimal increase in electron screening. Consequently, the effective nuclear charge (\(Z_{\mathrm{eff}}\)) increases across the period, pulling the valence electron cloud closer to the nucleus and steadily reducing the atomic size.

Therefore, the decrease in atomic radius across the period is primarily due to the increasing effective nuclear charge that outweighs the shielding effect while electrons enter the same principal quantum shell.

answer.text: Electrons are added to the same principal quantum shell and the increasing nuclear charge outweighs the shielding effect.
The principal quantum number of the valence electrons decreases steadily with increasing atomic number.
Inner core electron shielding increases more rapidly than the nuclear charge across the period.
Interelectronic repulsion in the \(2p\) subshell dominates over the nuclear electrostatic attraction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q02 - Ionization enthalpy anomalies across second period

questiontext.text:
The diagram below displays the first ionization enthalpies (\(\Delta_i H\)) of elements of the second period as a function of atomic number (\(Z\)):

Points P and Q mark notable deviations where the ionization enthalpy drops below that of the immediately preceding element. Which combination correctly identifies elements P and Q along with the primary reason for the drop at Q?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify elements at points P and Q
In the second period graph, point P corresponds to atomic number \(Z = 5\) (Boron, \(\Delta_i H = 801\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) and point Q corresponds to atomic number \(Z = 8\) (Oxygen, \(\Delta_i H = 1314\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 2: Analysis of the deviation at Boron (Point P)
In beryllium (\(1s^2 2s^2\)), the electron is removed from a fully filled \(2s\) orbital which penetrates closer to the nucleus. In boron (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^1\)), the electron is detached from a \(2p\) orbital that is more shielded and penetrates less than a \(2s\) orbital, resulting in a lower \(\Delta_i H\) value for boron.

Step 3: Analysis of the deviation at Oxygen (Point Q)
Nitrogen (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\)) has an extra-stable half-filled \(2p\) subshell with three unpaired electrons residing in separate orbitals. In oxygen (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^2 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\)), two of the four \(2p\) electrons are paired in the same orbital. Mutual repulsion between these two paired electrons facilitates the removal of the fourth electron, causing the ionization enthalpy of oxygen to be lower than that of nitrogen.

Therefore, the element at point P is Boron, the element at point Q is Oxygen, and the drop at oxygen occurs because mutual repulsion between paired electrons in a \(2p\) orbital makes electron removal easier compared to the half-filled \(2p\) subshell of nitrogen.

answer.text: P is Carbon, Q is Fluorine; electron removal from Q leaves an unstable non-octet state.
P is Boron, Q is Oxygen; paired electrons in one of the \(2p\) orbitals of Q experience increased electron-electron repulsion.
P is Beryllium, Q is Nitrogen; Q has a half-filled \(2p\) configuration that releases energy upon ionization.
P is Boron, Q is Oxygen; Q possesses a higher effective nuclear charge that strongly repels valence electrons.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q03 - Atomic radius comparison of periodic families

questiontext.text:
The graph below illustrates the variation of atomic radius with atomic number (\(Z\)) for alkali metals (Group 1) and halogens (Group 17):

Based on the graph, which of the following statements provides the correct reasoning for why the alkali metal curve lies significantly above the halogen curve across all corresponding periods?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the vertical displacement between the curves
The diagram shows that for any given period, the alkali metal (Group 1) has a much larger atomic radius than the corresponding halogen (Group 17) in the same period (e.g., Li = 152 pm vs F = 72 pm; Na = 186 pm vs Cl = 99 pm).

Step 2: Compare effective nuclear charges across the period
Within any period, the alkali metal has the lowest atomic number and the smallest nuclear charge for that principal quantum level (\(n\)). As one moves across to the halogen, protons are progressively added to the nucleus while electrons enter the same principal valence shell.

Step 3: Evaluate electrostatic attraction on valence electrons
Because inner core shielding remains nearly identical across the same period, the effective nuclear charge (\(Z_{\mathrm{eff}}\)) increases to a maximum at the halogens. Consequently, valence electrons in halogens experience much stronger inward electrostatic attraction toward the nucleus, contracting the electron cloud and giving halogens substantially smaller atomic radii than alkali metals.

Therefore, within each period, alkali metals have the lowest effective nuclear charge and experience the weakest nuclear pull on outermost electrons, whereas halogens have the highest effective nuclear charge pulling the valence shell tightly inward.

answer.text: Halogens possess a higher principal quantum number than alkali metals in the same period.
Alkali metals have more filled inner core electron shells than halogens belonging to the same period.
Alkali metals experience the minimum effective nuclear charge in their respective periods, whereas halogens experience the maximum attraction pulling the valence shell inward.
Interelectronic repulsion between valence electrons is significantly greater in alkali metals than in halogens.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q04 - Periodic table overview of property trends

questiontext.text:
The schematic diagram below summarizes major periodic trends across periods and down groups of the Periodic Table:

In this summary chart, each directional arrow indicates an increasing trend of the respective atomic property. Which pair correctly identifies Property X (which increases from left to right across a period) and Property Y (which increases from top to bottom down a group)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify trends across a period (Property X)
Moving from left to right across a period, effective nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases. As valence electrons are held more tightly, Electronegativity, Ionization Enthalpy, and Non-metallic character increase, while Atomic Radius and Metallic character decrease.

Step 2: Identify trends down a group (Property Y)
Moving from top to bottom down a vertical group, successive principal energy levels are added, increasing the distance of valence electrons from the nucleus and providing greater electron shielding. Consequently, Atomic Radius and Metallic character increase down a group, whereas Electronegativity and Ionization Enthalpy decrease.

Step 3: Correlate properties with labels X and Y
Property X points horizontally across a period from left to right (increasing electronegativity, ionization enthalpy, or electron gain enthalpy). Property Y points vertically down a group from top to bottom (increasing atomic radius or metallic character). Therefore, matching Property X as Electronegativity and Property Y as Atomic Radius satisfies both directional vectors shown in the diagram.

Therefore, Property X corresponds to Electronegativity (or Ionization Enthalpy) and Property Y corresponds to Atomic Radius (or Metallic Character).

answer.text: Property X: Atomic Radius; Property Y: Electronegativity
Property X: Metallic Character; Property Y: Ionization Enthalpy
Property X: Atomic Radius; Property Y: Metallic Character
Property X: Electronegativity; Property Y: Atomic Radius

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q05 - Periodic peaks and troughs in ionization enthalpy

questiontext.text:
The plot below shows the variation of first ionization enthalpy (\(\Delta_i H\)) with atomic number (\(Z\)) for the first 20 elements:

Which statement accurately analyzes the physical causes for the sharp maxima occurring at helium, neon, and argon, and the deep minima occurring at lithium, sodium, and potassium in the ionization enthalpy curve?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Characterize the elements occupying the maxima
The sharp maxima in the ionization enthalpy plot occur at helium (\(1s^2\)), neon (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\)), and argon (\([Ne] 3s^2 3p^6\)). These elements possess completely filled, closed electronic shells with maximum stability and large effective nuclear charge, requiring tremendous energy to detach an electron.

Step 2: Characterize the elements occupying the minima
The deep minima occur at lithium (\([He] 2s^1\)), sodium (\([Ne] 3s^1\)), and potassium (\([Ar] 4s^1\)). In each case, an electron enters a new principal quantum shell farther from the nucleus, preceded by a stable noble gas core.

Step 3: Comparative evaluation of shielding and nuclear pull
For alkali metals, the intervening core electrons effectively screen the nucleus, leaving the single outermost \(s\)-electron weakly held and easily ionizable. In contrast, noble gases experience the peak effective nuclear charge of their periods without any outer shielding electrons, making their ionization enthalpies exceptionally high.

Therefore, noble gases exhibit maxima due to stable, completely filled closed valence shells and high effective nuclear charge, whereas alkali metals exhibit minima because their single outermost \(ns^1\) electron is located far from the nucleus and strongly shielded by the inner core.

answer.text: Maxima represent elements where electrons are removed from unstable half-filled subshells, whereas minima represent closed noble gas cores.

Maxima correspond to elements with stable closed valence electron shells and high effective nuclear charge, whereas minima correspond to elements having a single outermost \(s\)-electron screened by a noble gas core.
Maxima occur because noble gases have the largest atomic radii in their periods, requiring extra energy to compress the electron cloud.
Minima occur at alkali metals because pairing of electrons in the \(ns\) subshell causes severe interelectronic repulsion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q06 - Radius variation in ten electron isoelectronic series

questiontext.text:
The diagram below depicts the relationship between ionic radius (pm) and nuclear charge (\(Z\)) for an isoelectronic series containing 10 electrons (\(\mathrm{N^{3-}, O^{2-}, F^-, Na^+, Mg^{2+}, Al^{3+}}\)):

Which statement correctly explains why the ionic radius decreases progressively from \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) despite all species possessing identical numbers of electrons?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given data and conditions
All six species (\(\mathrm{N^{3-}, O^{2-}, F^-, Na^+, Mg^{2+}, Al^{3+}}\)) are isoelectronic, each possessing exactly 10 electrons in the ground state configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\). Their nuclear charges (\(Z\)) are 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 13 respectively.

Step 2: Analysis of the cation series
As nuclear charge increases from \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) (\(Z = 11\)) to \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 13\)), 10 electrons are attracted by an increasingly positive nucleus containing 11, 12, and 13 protons. The higher positive charge attracts the electron cloud more strongly toward the center, contracting the ionic radius progressively from 95 pm (\(\mathrm{Na^+}\)) to 53.5 pm (\(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\)).

Step 3: Analysis of the anion series
For anions (\(\mathrm{N^{3-}, O^{2-}, F^-}\)), the nuclear charge is smaller than the number of electrons (7, 8, and 9 protons attracting 10 electrons). In \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\), the lowest positive nuclear charge of +7 must hold 10 electrons, meaning net electron-electron repulsion outweighs the nuclear pull, causing maximum expansion of the ion.

Therefore, across this isoelectronic series, the progressive decrease in size from \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) is governed by the continuous increase in positive nuclear charge, which enhances electrostatic attraction on the fixed number of 10 electrons and draws them closer to the nucleus.

answer.text: The principal quantum level (\(n\)) of the outermost electrons decreases as the positive charge increases.
The screening effect of inner electrons increases rapidly with increasing atomic number in the isoelectronic series.
The positive nuclear charge increases from 7 to 13, pulling the same number of 10 electrons progressively closer to the nucleus.
The number of valence electrons decreases from \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\), leading to reduced electron-electron repulsion.
